title: Showcase challenge
goal: I can use ideas from all the units in a mixed challenge, and plan a small puzzle program: maths first, then blocks, then tests.

learn.intro: A good puzzle program starts with maths. Find the answer by hand first, then turn the rule into blocks, then test it with a number you already know the answer for.

example.problem: Plan a program. It asks for n and says the day n days after Monday. The list days holds Monday to Sunday.
steps: Idea: a week is a clock with 7 days, so we need n mod 7.
By hand: 10 days after Monday. 10 mod 7 = 3, so the day is Thursday.
Blocks: a list starts at item 1, so set r to n mod 7, then pos to r + 1.
Test with known values: n = 10 gives Thursday, n = 0 and n = 7 give Monday.
example.answer: The program says item 4 of days, Thursday, when n = 10.

howto.title: How to plan a puzzle program
steps: Pick a maths idea and find an answer by hand.
Turn the rule into blocks: input, rule, output.
Test with a value you know. Also try 0 or 1.
Add a twist, then explain why it works.

try.text: The user types 19. What does the program above say? {l}
try.explanation: 19 mod 7 = 5, because 19 = 2 × 7 + 5. pos = 5 + 1 = 6, and item 6 of days is Saturday.

items.text: A pattern uses 8, 14, 20, 26, ... tiles.
items.explanation: The difference is 6. Each term is 2 more than 6, 12, 18, 24, so the rule is 6n + 2. The 50th term is 6 × 50 + 2 = 302. 6n + 2 = 164 gives 6n = 162, so n = 27.

items.text: Mei's bank balance is −6 dollars, so she owes the bank. She pays in 15 dollars and then spends 20 dollars.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Later her balance goes from −6 to 21 dollars. It rises by {b} dollars.

items.explanation: −6 + 15 = 9. Then 9 − 20 = −11. From −6 up to 21 is 6 steps to 0 and 21 more: 27.

parts.text: A machine does × 5, then − 7. OUT is 43. IN = {b}

parts.label: a
parts.text: A menu has 3 starters, 5 mains and 2 drinks. A meal is one of each: {b} meals.

parts.label: b

items.text: Think about fair and likely.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bag has 5 red and 3 blue counters. P(red) = {b}/{b}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A dice is rolled 1200 times. About {b} of the rolls are 4s.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Ali wins on an even number. Ben wins on 1, 3 or 5. Is it fair?   {circ:Yes|No}

items.explanation: (a) 8 counters, 5 red: 5/8. (b) 1/6 × 1200 = 200. (c) An even number is 2, 4 or 6, and 1, 3 or 5 is the other 3 numbers: 3 out of 6 each, so the game is fair.

items.text: Each inside angle of a regular polygon is 165°.
items.explanation: The turn is 180 − 165 = 15°, and 360 ÷ 15 = 24 sides.

parts.label: a
parts.text: It is 4 o'clock. In 75 hours it is {b} o'clock.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Code MATH with a shift of 9: {l}

items.text: Averages.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A trip lasts 5 days. The mean distance is 13 km a day. On 4 days the distances are 9, 15, 12 and 17 km. On day 5 it is {b} km.

items.explanation: (a) The total is 5 × 13 = 65 km. 9 + 15 + 12 + 17 = 53, so day 5 is 12 km. (b) In order: 4, 9, 12, 15. The middle two are 9 and 12, so the median is halfway between them: 10.5.

items.text: A program runs: set n to 11, then repeat 25 times: change n by 6. Then it says n.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The rule for the sequence is {b} × n + {b}.

items.explanation: n goes 11, 17, 23, ... and after 25 jumps it is 11 + 25 × 6 = 161. From the 1st term to the 26th term is 25 jumps, so 161 is the 26th term. The rule is 6n + 5 (6 × 26 + 5 = 161).

items.text: A game starts with a score of 50. This code plays 8 rounds. Run it by hand.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The score first resets to 50 after round {b}.

items.explanation: Each round takes away 8: 42, 34, 26, 18. The score 18 is below 20, so it resets to 50 after round 4. Rounds 5 to 8 repeat the pattern: 42, 34, 26, 18, and the score resets to 50 again after round 8. After round 6 the score is 34.

items.text: The steps of planning a program are mixed up. A: Test with a value you know. B: Do the maths by hand. C: Build the blocks. D: Pick a maths idea. E: Add a twist.
items.explanation: You need an idea (D) before you can do the maths (B). You build the blocks (C) after the maths, test them (A) once they exist, and add a twist (E) when the basic version works.

items.text: Spinner A has the numbers 1 to 4 and spinner B has 1 to 3. Both are spun and the numbers are added. There are 12 equally likely results.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The spinners are spun 240 times. About {b} totals are 3.

items.explanation: A total of 3 comes from A = 1 and B = 2, or A = 2 and B = 1: 2 results. 2/12 = 1/6. 1/6 × 240 = 40.

items.text: A sprite starts at x = 15. It repeats 7 times: change x by −4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: x is below 0 for the first time after repeat {b}.

items.explanation: 7 moves of −4 make −28. 15 − 28 = −13. After 4 repeats x = 15 − 16 = −1, which is the first time below 0 (after 3 repeats x = 3).

items.text: A sequence has the rule 6n − 1. Look at its first 10 terms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: {b} of the first 10 terms are prime.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The one that is not prime is {b}.

items.hint: Write out the 10 terms. Test each for factors.
items.explanation: 5, 11, 17, 23, 29, 35, 41, 47, 53, 59. 35 = 5 × 7 is the only one that is not prime, so 9 of the 10 are prime. 6n is even and an even number take away 1 is odd, so every term is odd.

items.text: Ali has taken 5 tests. His mean score is 74. After the 6th test his mean is 76.

parts.label: b
parts.text: After the 6th test the total is {b}.

items.hint: Total = mean × how many. Do it for 5 tests and for 6.
items.explanation: The 5 tests total 5 × 74 = 370. The 6 tests total 6 × 76 = 456. The 6th score is 456 − 370 = 86.

items.text: A 2-digit number has digits that add to 10. Reversing its digits gives another 2-digit number.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The primes with digits that add to 10 are {l}

parts.label: b
parts.text: Those whose reverse is also prime are {b} and {b}.

items.hint: List all numbers with digit sum 10. Cross out the non-primes.
items.explanation: Digits adding to 10: 19, 28, 37, 46, 55, 64, 73, 82, 91. Primes: 19, 37, 73. Reversed: 91 = 7 × 13 is not prime, but 73 and 37 both are.

items.text: A taxi costs 7 dollars for 2 km and 16 dollars for 5 km, by one rule.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A fare of 49 dollars is a ride of {b} km.

items.hint: How many km apart are 2 km and 5 km? How much more is the fare?
items.explanation: From 2 km to 5 km is 3 km more, and the fare rises by 16 − 7 = 9 dollars, so each km costs 9 ÷ 3 = 3 dollars. Then 7 = 3 × 2 + 1, so there is a 1 dollar start fee. The rule is n × 3 + 1. A 20 km ride costs 3 × 20 + 1 = 61 dollars. A fare of 49 dollars means 3n = 48, so n = 16.

items.text: A spinner has 8 parts numbered 1 to 8. A program spins it 800 times and counts the numbers greater than 6.

parts.label: c
parts.text: If the test were greater than 3, it would say about {b}.

items.hint: Count the numbers that pass the test.
items.explanation: The numbers greater than 6 are 7 and 8, which is 2 results out of 8, so 1/4. 1/4 × 800 = 200. The numbers greater than 3 are 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8, which is 5 out of 8, so the count would be 5/8 × 800 = 500. A real run is near these numbers, not exactly equal.

items.text: This code stops when n reaches 1. Run it by hand.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Starting at 7, the largest value n takes is {b}.

items.explanation: n = 6: 6, 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. That is 8 steps (halve if even, or 3n + 1 if odd). n = 7: 7, 22, 11, 34, 17, 52, 26, 13, 40, 20, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 is 16 steps. The largest number reached from 7 is 52.
The difference is 4. Each term is 1 less than 4, 8, 12, 16, so the rule is 4n − 1.

items.text: A bag holds 7 red counters and 8 blue counters. P(red) = {b}/{b} in simplest form.
items.explanation: 7 red out of 15 counters is 7/15, which is already in simplest form.

items.text: It is 3 o'clock. In 100 hours it will be {b} o'clock.
items.explanation: 3 + 100 = 103. 103 mod 12 = 7, because 8 × 12 = 96. It will be 7 o'clock.
